description: COSE cross-signing conformance (RFC 9052 / 9053 / 9338 / 9679). Every case is signed by both implementations and then handed to the other one to verify. Signing is deterministic on both sides, because that is the only mode in which two implementations can be compared byte for byte; the randomized mode is exercised by the cross-verification instead. Deterministic means a different thing in each family: RFC 6979 for ECDSA, nothing to arrange for EdDSA, the zero-randomness variant of FIPS 204 for ML-DSA, and a salt of zeroes for RSASSA-PSS. The keys are the example keys of RFC 9052, of the specification's worked example and, where no published example covers what a row needs — the brainpool curves, and RSA, for which the COSE working group published no example at all — fixed keys of this suite's own. They secure nothing.

cases.description: A CBOR payload written in reading order rather than in the deterministic encoding of RFC 8949 §4.2.1 — {"meter": …, "time": …}, whose sorted spelling puts "time" first. Both implementations rewrite it before signing, so the message carries the sorted 49 bytes and not the 49 bytes handed in. The point is what happens afterwards: a receiver that decodes the record and encodes it again produces the sorted form, and unless the signer produced it too, that receiver forwards a signature that no longer verifies — having altered nothing. This vector is what makes the two implementations agree about which of the two spellings gets signed.
The plain case: ECDSA with the curve taken from the key, algorithm in the protected bucket, key identifier in the unprotected one.
A 96-byte signature, and SHA-384.
P-521: a 66-byte group order, a 132-byte signature and a private key whose leading octet is zero. The case a big-integer serialization gets wrong.
The fully-specified algorithm of RFC 9864, which names its own curve rather than leaving it to the key.
The meter's algorithm in the worked example: brainpoolP256r1, registered for COSE by ISO/IEC 18013-5.

brainpoolP320r1, which the TypeScript side's curve library does not ship and which is therefore defined there from the domain parameters of RFC 5639 Section 3.4. Byte agreement with Bouncy Castle's own brainpoolP320r1 is what proves that transcription — a single wrong hex digit in p, a, b, n, Gx or Gy gives a curve that works perfectly and is not this one. Note the 320-bit curve paired with SHA-384, which RFC 9864 registers deliberately and which is also the hash the RFC 6979 nonce is derived with.

brainpoolP384r1 with SHA-384. The curve library ships this one, so unlike brainpoolP320r1 it is not a transcription under test; what is under test is that both implementations agree byte for byte on a 96-byte signature over a 384-bit brainpool curve, and that they pair the curve with the same hash. Registered for COSE by RFC 9864 and implemented on both sides since before this vector existed, which is what made the gap invisible.
brainpoolP512r1 with SHA-512, the widest brainpool curve either implementation offers: a 64-byte group order, a 128-byte signature, and an RFC 6979 nonce derived with SHA-512 rather than SHA-384.

RFC 9864's fully-specified algorithm for P-384, signing with the same key and the same hash as sign1-es384-p384 above. The signature is not the same one: the alg label sits in the protected bucket that the Sig_structure covers, so naming the curve in the algorithm rather than leaving it to the key changes the bytes being signed. Until this vector only ESP256 had one, and the registry recommends all three.

The same for P-521, on the key whose leading octet is zero — so it reads the big-integer serialization of sign1-es512-p521 a second time, under the label that names the curve. ESP512 pairs P-521 with SHA-512, which is what ES512 does with this key anyway: the computation is the same and only the protected header differs.
secp256k1, whose signatures are the ones most often normalized to the low-S form by libraries that should not.

EdDSA on Ed25519 (RFC 8032, RFC 9864): a pure scheme, which signs the Sig_structure itself rather than a digest of it, on a key of key type OKP where the public key is the whole of x and there is no y. Deterministic by construction — the nonce comes from the key and the message — so the byte comparison needs no arrangement at all. The private key is the one of RFC 8032 Section 7.1, TEST 1.

EdDSA on Ed448, whose keys are 57 bytes and not 56 — RFC 8032 appends a sign bit to the 456-bit encoding — and whose signature is 114 bytes. The private key is the 'Blank' vector of RFC 8032 Section 7.4.

The key, the key identifier and the payload of sign1-ed25519 above, under the identifier that algorithm was registered with before RFC 9864 arrived: EdDSA (-8), which names no curve and leaves it to the key. That is what the registry now marks Deprecated and what RFC 9864 replaced with Ed25519 (-19) and Ed448 (-53) — and it is also why this row comes as a pair rather than alone. ES256, ES384 and ES512 are three deprecated identifiers for three curves, each fixing its own hash; -8 is one identifier for both EdDSA curves, so a verifier has nowhere to read the curve from but the key. An implementation that resolved -8 to Ed25519 once and for all verifies this message and fails the one below it. Deprecating the identifier does not retire the messages that carry it, which is the reason to hold both sides to reading it at all.

The other half of that pair: the same -8 over the Ed448 key of sign1-ed448, where the curve the identifier does not name is the one that makes the signature 114 bytes instead of 64. Nothing in the protected bucket distinguishes this message from the one above except the key it was signed with, which is the whole of what -8 says and the whole of what RFC 9864 objects to.

ML-DSA-44 (FIPS 204, RFC 9964): the post-quantum scheme, on a key of key type AKP whose labels -1 and -2 are the public and the private key rather than the curve and the x coordinate. The private key is the 32-byte seed, as RFC 9964 requires, and both sides sign in the deterministic variant of FIPS 204 — the one where the per-signature randomness is 32 zero bytes — because the RFC leaves the choice open and it is the choice that decides whether bytes can be compared.
ML-DSA-65: a 1952-byte public key and a 3309-byte signature.

The strongest parameter set over a tag-44252 reading — (1234.567 ±12.3) kWh, k=2, p=0.95, dist=normal — which is where the two halves of this project meet. A 4627-byte signature over 31 bytes of measurement is what post-quantum costs, and it is the argument for carrying it in CBOR: in JSON the signature would travel as base64 and grow by a further third, on the largest field in the message.

RSASSA-PSS with SHA-256 [RFC 8230], the first RSA row this suite ever had and the one the registry recommends. These six algorithms were the asymmetry FINDINGS Section 28 counted on 2026-11-03: Styx implemented them, COSE.TS did not, and no cross-implementation vector can ask for what only one side can do. PSS is randomized by design — the salt is as long as the hash and travels inside the signature, recovered by whoever verifies and never compared with anything [RFC 8017, Section 9.1.2] — so these bytes are comparable at all only because both implementations take a salt of zeroes when asked for deterministic output. That is the same departure from default settings this suite makes for ECDSA (RFC 6979) and for ML-DSA (the deterministic variant of FIPS 204), and it costs less here than there: a repeated PSS salt reveals nothing about the key and no verifier can tell it apart from a random one, while a repeated ECDSA nonce is fatal. The key is a fixed 2048-bit one of this suite's own, which is the width RFC 8230 Section 6.1 requires as a minimum, printed with all eight parameters of its Section 4 because a COSE key carries all eight and no scalar derives them. It secures nothing.

The middle hash, which moves three things at once against the row above: a 48-byte digest, a 48-byte salt, and a mask generated with SHA-384 — RFC 8230 Section 2 fixes the mask generation function to MGF1 and recommends the same hash for both, which this suite follows because the specification does. The encoded block stays 256 bytes with its leftmost bit cleared, so that the integer it becomes is certainly smaller than the modulus; what changes inside it is the length of the salt and of the digest, and the zero padding that makes up the difference.

The widest hash, and the row where the padding nearly runs out: 64 bytes of digest, 64 of salt, 8 zero octets of the PSS prefix and one trailer leave 126 of the 256 bytes of the encoded block. With a 1024-bit modulus this scheme would not fit at all — 128 bytes cannot hold 130 — which is one way of reading the key size RFC 8230 Section 6.1 requires: the algorithms of that document do not merely prefer a wide key, the widest of them has no room in a narrow one.

RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 with SHA-256 [RFC 8812], registered Not Recommended and present for the reason it is registered at all: it is what WebAuthn authenticators and TPMs offer when they offer RSA. Its encoded block is 0x00 0x01, then 0xFF octets, then 0x00, then a DER DigestInfo wrapping the digest — the one place in COSE where a signature carries an ASN.1 structure. There is no salt and no randomness of any kind, so the two implementations agree byte for byte with nothing arranged, which makes this the plainest signature row in the suite. What it pins is the 19-byte prefix: hard-coded in COSE.TS from the note in RFC 8017 Section 9.2, produced by Bouncy Castle in Styx, and identical in both or this row is red.

The same padding with the second of the three prefixes. Three octets separate them: the length of the outer SEQUENCE, the last byte of the hash OID — 2.16.840.1.101.3.4.2.1, .2.2, .2.3 for the three SHA-2 widths — and the length of the digest the DigestInfo wraps. Both implementations verify by re-encoding the block and comparing it rather than by parsing the DER a signature hands them, which is the lesson of Bleichenbacher's 2006 forgeries: a parser that accepts a DigestInfo with trailing rubbish accepts a signature nobody made.

The third prefix, and with it every RSA row of the registry that both implementations implement. 2048 bits of modulus, 512 bits of digest: the signature is the same 256 bytes as every other row here, because the width of an RSA signature is the width of the modulus and says nothing about the hash inside it. That is worth one row of its own, since it is the property that lets an implementation accept a signature of the right size and the wrong algorithm without noticing — and what stops it is that the digest is covered twice over, once by the algorithm label in the protected bucket and once inside the encoded block.

A key with three prime factors rather than two — the multi-prime form of RFC 8230 Section 4, whose further primes travel as an array at label −9, each a map of r_i, d_i and t_i at −10, −11 and −12. The section offers the form without requiring it of anybody ("the document also provides support for the so-called 'multi-prime' RSA keys"), so the two implementations would be free to differ here. They did, and no longer do: COSE.TS signed with the key first, and Styx refused it in so many words, keeping the array for the round trip; since Styx 244aa8c3 both sign, through the multi-prime steps of RFC 8017 Section 5.1.2, and each verifies the other's message. The row stays `survey` because the form stays optional. What it holds both of them to besides is the identity: RFC 9679 takes kty, n and e and nothing else, so the further primes must not enter the thumbprint, and the thumbprint is recorded before anybody is asked to sign. RS256 rather than PS256 because RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 has no randomness at all, so the two signatures are directly comparable — and each side's own tests hold its bytes to a computation that is not its own: COSE.TS's to OpenSSL's, Styx's to the first form of RSASP1, m^d mod n, which needs no prime at all. The key was generated once by OpenSSL (`genrsa -primes 3 2048`), because nothing else in reach generates one: three primes of 683, 683 and 682 bits and a 2048-bit modulus, which is Section 6.1's minimum. It secures nothing.
The CBOR tag is not covered by the signature, so the untagged message must carry the very same signature bytes as the tagged one.
A detached payload: the message carries nil, and the verifier has to be handed the payload separately.
Externally supplied additional authenticated data, which is signed without travelling in the message.
The leanest signed message: an empty protected bucket, the algorithm taken from the profile rather than from the message. The empty bucket must be h'' and never h'A0'.

The point of the whole exercise: the payload is a tag-44252 metrological value — (1234.567 ±12.3) kWh, k=2, p=0.95, dist=normal — signed by the meter's key. If the two CBOR codecs disagreed about one byte of this reading, neither signature would verify at the other implementation.

COSE_Sign (tag 98) with two independent signers on two different curves. Its Sig_structure has five elements rather than four, with each signature's own protected bucket between the body and the external data.
A COSE_Sign1 countersigned per RFC 9338: a signature of a signature, in the unprotected bucket, over a six-element structure whose last element is an array holding the body signature.

The migration message: one COSE_Sign carrying a classical and a post-quantum signature side by side, so that verifiers which know only ECDSA and verifiers which already require ML-DSA can both be satisfied by the same bytes. This is what a half-migrated fleet actually emits, and it is also where the two signature families meet inside one structure — a 64-byte signature and a 3309-byte one in the same array, over Sig_structures that differ only in the signer's own protected bucket.

Two pure schemes in one message: EdDSA and ML-DSA both sign the Sig_structure itself rather than a digest of it, and both codebases had the digest-based ECDSA shape hard-wired before they were widened. Two signers of different key types — OKP and AKP — also put the label collision to work in a single message, where -1 carries the curve for the one signer and the public key for the other.

The deployment that the quantum transition actually forces: a meter in the field signs its reading with the key it was manufactured with — brainpoolP256r1, as in the worked example — and cannot be replaced, so the gateway that receives the reading countersigns it with ML-DSA-87. The archive is then protected against an adversary the meter's own signature is not. Note that this leaves the body signature classical: the countersignature vouches for the message, it does not repair it.

The other direction, and the one that tests a structure rather than a scenario: an ML-DSA-87 body countersigned classically, which is the only case in this suite that puts a 4627-byte byte string into the other_fields element of the RFC 9338 version-2 countersignature structure. Everything else this suite countersigns fits the one-byte length form, 81 58 40; this crosses into the two-byte one, 81 59 1213, and an encoder that got that threshold wrong would be caught here and nowhere else.
